uncited: Run-length and palette-compressed bricks are a hybrid compression technique for voxel data that combines run-length encoding (RLE) with palette-based index compression to reduce memory footprint for material-heavy volumes.
It solves the problem of storing redundant material identifiers in large, homogeneous regions by mapping voxel values to a small palette and storing only indices.
**Palette:** An array of material definitions.
The size is determined by the number of unique materials in the brick.
**Index Array:** A bit-packed array storing indices into the palette.
The bit-depth per index is determined by the palette size (e.g., $\lceil \log_2(\text{palette\_size}) \rceil$ bits).
**Palette Extraction:** For each brick, identify all unique material IDs present.
Construct the palette from these unique IDs.
**Index Mapping:** Replace each voxel's material ID with its index in the local palette.
**Bit-Packing:** Pack the indices into a contiguous bit stream.
If the palette has $N$ entries, use $k = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ bits per index.
- Bits per index: $k = \lceil \log_2(\text{num\_unique\_materials}) \rceil$
- Total bits for indices: $B = \text{voxel\_count} \times k$
Palette compression mitigates this by allowing direct index lookup, though cache locality depends on index distribution.
- **Time Complexity:** Compression is $O(N)$ where $N$ is the number of voxels, dominated by palette extraction and bit-packing.
Decompression is $O(N)$ for bit-unpacking.
- **Memory Complexity:** Storage is proportional to $N \times \lceil \log_2(\text{unique\_materials}) \rceil$ bits plus palette overhead.
Significantly better than raw storage when material diversity is low.
- **When to use:** Terrain, building blocks, and volumes with discrete, repeating materials.
- **When not to use:** Volumes with high material entropy or requiring fine-grained per-voxel color variation without palette limits.
